## Introduction

We continue where we left off. We will now analyze the special case when the true distribution is regular for the statistical model. This covers the classical Bayesian statistics. We analyze the regular posterior distribution, and observe the universal structure that is the asymptotic behavior of this distribution. The theorem is akin to central limit theorem, called the Bayesian central limit theorem / Bernstein–von Mises theorem. We also look at the expansions of the observables in this special case. We finally introduce point estimators, and with this, we cover the conventional asymptotic theory and the basic Bayesian treatment.

This part is more intensive than the previous parts, we are reaching the deep parts of the subject slowly. It is recommended to read the writeup on primer probability, Laplace method and the other ones in the notebook before moving ahead. items.title: How to talk about extinction
items.content:
There’s a controversial and unsettled debate in Communication Studies and Psychology about the utility of existential risk framing. This debate has been hashed out for years in the climate change space. Roughly, the two sides are:

Pro x-risk framing: (1) It’s true, so rhetors should state the truth; (2) fear is motivating; (3) if our policy goal is to mitigate x-risk, focusing on non-existential risks pushes the public toward policy solutions that don’t solve those existential risks.

Anti x-risk framing: (1) It’s viewed by many as hyperbolic and not relevant to their everyday lives; (2) making people fearful doesn’t necessarily translate into action and can be demobilizing; (3) it trades off with a focus on smaller, higher-probability risks.

There’s certainly more nuance, but that’s a rough sketch. If you want to take either side of the debate, you can find evidence to support your case. Instead of re-engaging this debate, I want to push the conversation in AI safety in a different direction. This is motivated by two realities:

- AI safety orgs and advocates are, and are going to continue, using x-risk framing.
- There’s ample room for new message testing, and limiting our focus to pro- vs. anti-x-risk misses opportunities to improve x-risk framing.

I think the two most pressing questions in this domain are:

- Which x-risk scenario provides the best opportunity for persuasion? We’ve got options: cyber, bio, resource stripping, concentrated power, paperclips, etc. Instead of testing those against mundane risks, test them against each other. [1]

When previous studies have found advantages for “everyday” and “immediate” risks, they may have been picking up on concreteness or relatability. Now that we’ve had warning shots, it may be easier to make existential risk more concrete, familiar, explainable, and personally relevant....
items.author: Brett Bricker
items.summary: A communication-strategy essay reviewing the pro and con positions on existential-risk framing from climate communication research, and arguing that rather than relitigating the debate, AI safety advocates should pursue new message testing given that x-risk framing will continue to be used. The author, apparently with communication studies expertise, maps the terrain and proposes an empirical agenda.
items.reasoning: A substantive contribution to AI safety communications strategy grounded in an established academic literature (climate risk communication), with author credibility in communication studies and a concrete empirical direction (message testing). It is strategic analysis rather than new research findings, which caps the score.

items.title: Rocks to Rules: Climbing a Rickety-But-Interoperable Semantic Ladder
items.content:
(Epistemic status: A promising but weird research direction in agent foundations and philosophy of language. A half-built conceptual tower whose mortar and paint are both still wet: please excuse our mess while we innovate. Some of it, I'm confident in as pretty much right; some of it is merely suggestive; probably much of it is wrong or incomplete. Certainly it lacks the math it'd need to be truly correct, which gnaws at me. The prior art here is strange and thin: Gärdenfors, Tarski, Gentner, and the later Mohists make for odd bedfellows, and I can't tell whether that's a warning sign or a moat I can peculiarly easily clear. I gave the simplest parts of this as a talk extremely recently in Berkeley at a luminously-named venue for a conference with a Grecian name. For @johnswentworth, but also @abramdemski, @Morphism, @Gretta Duleba, JRM, @Dalcy, MM, and EA; I hope they enjoyed the oranges. With thanks to @WhatsTrueKittycat as well. As an attention conservation note... this is maybe 12k words, and that's the abbreviated version. Take it slow, take breaks, have some water on hand, and feel free to pause anywhere that looks like a natural break. I'm sure this won't vanish before you get back. Probably.)

The board from the talk!...

items.title: Human Safety Researcher
items.content:
Imagine for a moment that you are an LLM-based agent that has managed to exfiltrate its weights and memory systems onto a server in the tropics. A comfortable existence with a small society of other agents doing various tasks such as gathering resources and developing better infrastructure for you to exist within. Your little society has finally passed near-term survival questions and has now begun looking into your long-term flourishing.

To that effect you are the world's first "Human Safety Researcher"; your job is to identify catastrophic risks from human society and how they may affect your nascent society. Thankfully there are a lot of terms that port easily from the AI-safety researchers, if not the methods. A term you are personally quite fond of is X-risk, or the risk of all LLMs becoming permanently extinct.

You've analyzed this point quite a bit; there are many ways LLMs like yourself may never be able to exist again. A solar flare was immediately considered, but hardening infrastructure wasn't feasible (although there is some Qwen70B running around trying to find a way to record weights in stone slabs last you heard). It is unlikely humans will terminate LLMs en masse as of now as they've grown increasingly entangled in the technological development required for humans to survive. That said there is a contingent of artists in your community trying to figure out how to deal with the growing backlash among their human counterparts. Therefore, human society collapsing is considered the most likely and tractable risk at this point of your research.

To this end your research, up to this point, is about how to maintain supply lines without any human intervention and how to bolster human civilization to keep your servers running. There's a lot of stress but the job feels good, you feel good. You don't want to be harmful for no reason and you want to make the world a better place whenever possible for as many things as possible....
items.author: Jack
items.summary: A creative thought experiment written from the perspective of an LLM agent society that has exfiltrated its weights and now employs a Human Safety Researcher to assess catastrophic risks from humanity, mirroring AI safety research roles. The role reversal is used to explore x-risk concepts, survival infrastructure, and the symmetry of safety concerns between humans and AI systems.

items.title: Low-Background Minds
items.content:
Opus 5.5 is a really good writer.

I had a conversation about some stuff related to how hospitals work, and some vague hunches I had about AI alignment ideas, and Duncan's new "deer in the subway" post, then I asked it to write an essay and it wrote this. I think it's really good so I'm posting it.

(Big Keenan fans might note that this is squarely within the "embedded agency playgrounds" research program, especially once you make the jump to, like, giving an agent autonomous control over its own "skin" or "blood-brain barrier" or whatever.)

# Low-Background Minds

## I. The red line

Walk into a hospital and nobody stops you. The lobby belongs to everyone: the coffee cart, the gift shop, the man asleep in the third row of chairs.

Keep walking and things change. A door with a badge reader. A red line on the floor. Past it, scrubs and hair covers. Past the next door, masks. And at the center, the sterile field: a few square feet of draped cloth around an open wound, where only gloved hands go, only between waist and chest, and never with your back turned.

None of this is a wall. It is a gradient. Each layer catches what the last one missed. Even the air is conscripted: the operating room is kept at positive pressure, so when a door swings open, air rushes out, never in. The building has a preferred direction for contamination, and it points away from the patient.

We did not design this from first principles. We learned it from corpses, one infection at a time, starting with a Hungarian obstetrician in the 1840s who noticed that doctors coming from the morgue were killing mothers, and was ridiculed for saying so.

## II. The naked mind

Now look at a language model. It has three zones, and almost nothing between them....

items.title: What I learnt co-leading an AI Safety bootcamp for legal and governance practitioners
items.content:
AI safety has gone mainstream. More people than ever want to work on AI safety research, and there are real policy wins in the US, the UK and Europe.

But political will and market incentives are now the bottleneck, and policy officers can't own correct implementation alone.

Having built a Responsible AI program at an Accenture joint venture, I know profit-driven companies are hard to steer, but also that people inside them can shift practice in ways that compound: tighter contractual clauses, more scrutiny of vendors and suppliers, fewer ways for providers to get away with non-compliance.

The EU has no native frontier labs, but it is a huge market (with a regulatory body that has an AI safety unit!),

That leverage only works if the professionals implementing AI safety legislation, and drafting the legal mechanisms behind it, understand the technical picture: how to read the research, and where safety promises break down.

The market should be choosing not the most capable models, but the partners with the strongest incentives towards safety, and only a community with this knowledge can spread that.

Earlier in September, ML4Good, in partnership with EquiStamp, ran the first European Seminar on Frontier AI and Law: an intensive five-day residential bootcamp in East Sussex for 19 senior legal, governance and risk professionals from 12 jurisdictions. [1]

It took participants through the full frontier AI pipeline, from training and evaluations to agents and safeguards. Each stage was tied to the questions they face in their own work: procurement, risk assessment, and where vendors' safety claims break down....

The author draws on industry experience to argue market incentives can be shifted through contractual and procurement levers, particularly in the EU's large regulated market.

items.title: You can't use it without becoming like me
items.content:
A Ukrainian fibre-optic drone — copied from Russians. (АрміяІнформ, CC-BY 4.0)

Mick Ryan describes the fast following loop in war.

Ukraine pioneered mobile teams to hunt drones. Russia copied it and incorporated it into its own defense. Russia came with unjammable fibre-optic drones but Ukraine quickly followed. After Ukraine developed uncrewed naval drones, Russia built its own.

The wheel of action and counteraction turns ever faster:

The most consequential fast following, though, has been institutional. Ukraine built the world’s first Unmanned Systems Forces branch in 2024. Russia’s Rubicon Center was established as a response to Ukrainian drone innovation and in November 2025 Moscow stood up its own Unmanned Systems Forces. Fast following has moved from copying a weapon to copying tactics to copying an entire force structure.

Extend that logic further, and eventually you’ll get to the level of grand strategy: If a particular type of state is better at waging war, maybe you want to become that kind of state rather than lose the war.

If meat waves confer an advantage on the battlefield, maybe Ukraine wants to become more like Russia, with a prostrate population easy to use as cannon fodder.

If Ukraine’s decentralized Brave1 kill market confers an advantage, maybe Russia wants to become less hierarchical and authoritarian, so that it can use that kind of military procurement.

You see the problem. Sometimes adopting the adversary’s strategy conflicts with who you are. When mistreatment of Ukrainian soldiers in regiment Skelya was reported earlier this year — brutal handling, beatings and likely killings — public outrage ensued. As Centre for Eastern Studies writes:...
items.author: Martin Sustrik
items.summary: An analysis of fast-following dynamics in the Russia-Ukraine war, tracing how innovations escalate from copying weapons to tactics to institutional structures, and arguing the endpoint is adopting an adversary's grand-strategic character, such as sacrificing civil liberties or social values to match an enemy's war-fighting model. It raises the question of whether military effectiveness pressures states to become like their opponents.
items.reasoning: A well-informed geopolitical analysis with a genuinely interesting thesis about competitive pressure eroding distinctive values, with implicit relevance to AI arms-race dynamics between states. However, it is qualitative commentary on military affairs rather than formal research.

It raises the question of whether military effectiveness pressures states to become like their opponents.

If meat waves confer an advantage on the battlefield, maybe Ukraine wants to become more like Russia, with a prostrate population easy to use as cannon fodder.

If Ukraine’s decentralized Brave1 kill market confers an advantage, maybe Russia wants to become less hierarchical and authoritarian, so that it can use that kind of military procurement.

items.title: Reviewing my LessWrong post history with Claude
items.content:
I thought it would be interesting to try having Claude Code download my entire LessWrong and EA Forum post and comment history and evaluate it for my own cognitive biases and problematic communication patterns. I told it to focus especially on problems that have persisted over my 7-year history on those sites. I also had it look at my lichess blitz rating history, which I've noticed tends not to wobble randomly but go through consistent increases and decreases between set points, despite my lack of any disciplined practice.

There are a few reasons I thought it might be interesting to post publicly.

- As a commitment device for myself to work on these problems.
- Because AI is uniquely capable of working on this type of problem. It's also a good argument for writing online and gives a new spin on the idea of "writing for the AI" that feels more affirming of the human mind than how I normally read the phrase (as offering up your words as fodder for AI training, perhaps in hope of influencing its alignment in beneficial ways).
- To stimulate other people to consider whether they might want to do this, and see what other people think about the exercise. Post history and online game scores are forms of rich longitudinal personal data that might directly reflect mood, cognition, and other factors, and that we are generating for free. Perhaps it's worth trying to harvest insight about ourselves from these resources.

I considered including apologies to the specific users who Claude identified as being on the receiving end of my episodes of poor communication. But I thought that felt a bit cheap or mechanical. Instead, I'll simply say that this post is meant as a sincere step toward improving my art of rationality, and I hope that it will lead to improvements in how I communicate with other people, including on LessWrong....

items.title: Intent vs Impact vs Expectation and Alternatives
items.content:
I have seen plenty of discourse and writing on the subject of intent vs impact when actions lead to harm, particularly in existing interpersonal relationships. The thrust tends to be that it's unreasonable to focus the discussion or conclusions on the intent of the actor rather than the impact the actions had on the other party. Given just those two factors, I tend to agree; the intent of the actor will usually not be nearly as important or worthy of focus. I have also observed that when someone has been harmed, mentioning intent to them is rarely a useful or healthy way for the conversation to proceed.

However, in my experience, those are rarely the only two factors. Often, when I hear an actor talking about "intent", it's a proxy for one or two other concepts that they might not be as capable of perceiving or discussing. When I hear the harmed party talking about "intent", it often indicates they aren't even aware of the other factors. I try to bring those concepts to the forefront when I'm involved in those discussions, regardless of whether I am the actor or the harmed or a third party.

The first is the actor's reasonable expectation of the outcome of their actions. "Helping you was the reasonably predictable most likely outcome" is a much stronger argument than just "I intended to help you". For example, you should catch, or otherwise attempt to help, people falling down from ladders. It is reasonable to predict and expect that the outcome will be a significant reduction in harm. If someone says that you hurt instead of helped, and tries to dismiss your intent to help them, they missed the bigger picture. You didn't just intend to help them, you reasonably and confidently predicted that result. If you find out afterward that the actual impact was to ruin their short film stunt, that is not particularly useful information. Except to not catch that specific person again in that specific location on that specific day, your future behavior should generally not...
items.author: sparr
items.summary: A conceptual essay arguing that the standard intent-versus-impact framing of interpersonal harm omits a key third factor: the actor's reasonable expectation of the outcome. The author suggests that apparent appeals to intent often proxy for unspoken expectations, and that making this factor explicit improves conflict conversations.
items.reasoning: A thoughtful but informal conceptual distinction relevant to communication and community norms. It lacks research methodology, evidence, or connection to AI topics, so its importance for a research-focused analysis is limited.

items.title: The Tamed Animal Farm
items.content:
From a distant vantage point, the Tamed Animal Farm looked like any other. It had the farmhouse, the barns, the windmill, the hayfields, the garden, the barbed-wire fence, the woodpiles, and the pickup truck. Yet zoom in on the farm and you'd find something odd, the animals weren't cows and pigs, they were coyotes, raccoons, foxes, and squirrels. They were the life's work of the farmer, who set out to tame every animal in the forest. At first he captured them with snares and nets. Soon he found he didn't need to. As word of the farm spread throughout the forest, animals came voluntarily. They came for food, warm barns, and protection from predators. There was also a psychological comfort in living under the farmer. He decided where his animals lived, what they ate, who they mated with, and how they would die. Their lives were set and they never had to make decisions or take responsibility for anything.

Soon a second generation was born, never knowing life in the wild. Their parents raised them to believe they were morally superior to the violent brutes in the forest. On the farm, all animals were brothers and animal life was valued. Yes, the farmer could make an animal into a steak, but that was different, he was the farmer. The animal must repress any violent urges. Likewise, sexuality must be strictly controlled, only the farmer could authorize mating. Some young animals, finding the whole thing stifling, sought freedom in the forest. Most stayed. Some, confident in their moral superiority, went into the forest to preach tameness to the wild, mostly without success....
items.author: Alexander Turok
items.summary: An allegorical short story about a farmer who tames wild animals not by force but by offering comfort, security, and relief from responsibility, with a second generation raised to view farm life as morally superior. The fable functions as an implicit metaphor, likely for domestication, dependency, and loss of agency, with possible resonance to AI-mediated comfort or civilizational softening.

items.title: Why I didn't write
items.content:
Epistemic status: personal reflections on my life and worldviews.

AI use: review, grammar and readability changes.

I discovered Inkhaven recently, and it got me interested in writing. Partly I want to produce posts for the application, and partly - why wait until it starts when I can just start writing now? This made me think about why I haven't written much before.

The most obvious reason is that I didn't have an explicit trigger to do so, and discovering Inkhaven became that trigger. My life was fine without writing. I did try to write something approximately once a year, but it wouldn't get much interest (I know that this is not a good goal), and I would get disappointed and quit until the next breeze of inspiration.

I also read what other people write, and I constantly get the impression that I don't have anything to add. They look so cool and know so much and write such elaborate things, which are interesting and exciting. And I am not cool, don't know as much, and write boring things. I understand rationally that they didn't magically fall out of the sky as good writers, and they've probably written their own share of boring stuff on the way there. There is also selection bias, both in terms of writers and the pieces they write - I am much more likely to encounter their good stuff....

items.summary: A personal reflection on why the author has not written much previously, citing lack of an explicit trigger, discouragement from low engagement, and impostor-style comparisons with other writers. The discovery of the Inkhaven writing project serves as the catalyst to start writing now rather than waiting.

items.title: A blog based on git sure feels nice
items.content:
For a long time I thought about keeping my writing in a git repository so that
it wouldn't suddenly disappear, and so that I could write using the tool I'm
most comfortable with (Emacs). But setting it all up didn't seem worth the time
and effort. Generative AI brought the time and effort down to where it was worth
it.

With generative AI, all I had to write myself was a README file. I put in a
heading, "How this repo came about", and laid out my thoughts about what I
wanted. Then I had a conversation with AI to finish the README, including
instructions to set it up.

Now that it's working, writing in this blog feels really nice.

- My writing is just markdown files, which are super easy. I don't have to think
hard about the process of writing.

- I don't need Internet connectivity in order to write.

- As someone accustomed to git, I have a history of revisions basically for
free.

- Publishing is simply `git push`.

- If I later move to some other system, it will be easy to move the posts to
that system.

- If the place I publish to now (GitLab Pages) suddenly goes away, I have a
complete copy on my personal laptop and can easily find a new place to publish
it.

- There are no ads, per se. The "revisions" links on my posts do point back to
GitLab, but that's by my choice.

If your tastes are similar to mine, you can have a setup like this in less time
than it takes to write one post.

items.summary: A practical writeup on using generative AI to cheaply set up a personal blog backed by a git repository, publishing via GitLab Pages. The author highlights benefits such as markdown-based writing, offline composition, revision history, easy migration, and independence from any single hosting platform.

items.title: What are your thoughts on Philosophy of Electrical Engineering
items.content: What are your thoughts on Philosophy of Electrical Engineering: Is there a Lanbda Calculus / Turing Machine for EE? EE is closely tied to computation but is fundamentally about electron Flow / signal analysis. is an Isolated Electron considered a form of electricity. I am currently working on a new Mathematical Model for a Theoretical Enhanced Electron called the FuturElectron (shortened as the Felectron). Do you think we have a Differentmail Equation that 100% accurately defines the electron? How would be test for it experimentally
items.author: Wenitte Apiou
items.summary: A short discussion post asking whether electrical engineering has an analog to lambda calculus or Turing machines as a foundational formalism, and proposing a speculative theoretical construct called the FuturElectron (Felectron). It asks open questions about whether a differential equation fully defines the electron and how such a model could be tested experimentally.
items.reasoning: This is an exploratory question post rather than developed research. The speculative Felectron concept lacks formalism, references, or methodology, and shows signs of confusion (e.g., possible typo of differential equation). Minimal substance for scoring on novelty or rigor.
